title: Erasmus
hook: a scholar who wanted reform by learning and gentleness

segments.voice: Yesterday, Utopia, written by Thomas More while trading jokes in Latin with Erasmus. Your line was witty and holy.

A farmer behind a plow, singing to himself as he works. A weaver at the loom, humming in time with the shuttle. A traveler on a long road, passing the miles with a story. Erasmus wrote that picture into the front of a book, and the songs he wanted them singing were the words of the Gospel, from their own memory, in their own tongue.
screen: `A FARMER SINGING AT THE PLOW.` → `A WEAVER HUMMING AT THE LOOM.` → `THE GOSPEL IN THEIR OWN TONGUE.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Erasmus worked from old Greek manuscripts of the New Testament and published the Greek text with his own Latin translation beside it, so readers could check the Latin against the language the apostles wrote in. That was his kind of reform: go back to the sources and read them carefully. Second, the preface. He called it the Paraclesis, an exhortation, and in it he paints that farmer, weaver and traveler. He wished the Gospels and Paul's letters were in every language, so ordinary people could know them by heart. Third, the gentleness. Erasmus saw plenty wrong in the Church of his day, and said so, often with jokes. But when Martin Luther broke with Rome, Erasmus did not follow him. He stayed Catholic, and when he finally disagreed with Luther in print, about whether the human will is free, he called his book a discussion, not an attack. Luther answered sharply, in a book of his own. Fourth, the hope underneath. Paul writes to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "And be not conformed to this world; but be reformed in the newness of your mind." Erasmus seems to have taken that line at its word: change the mind by giving it the text. Reform through learning, reading and patience, rather than anger. Whether it can always work that way is still an open question. He spent his life betting that it could.
screen: `GREEK AND LATIN, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE PARACLESIS: SCRIPTURE FOR ALL.` · `HE STAYED, AND DISAGREED GENTLY.` · `REFORMED IN THE NEWNESS OF YOUR MIND.` · then, large: `REFORM BY LEARNING.`

segments.voice: Choose one thing you want to change: a habit, a rule at work, a way your family talks to each other. Instead of planning a fight, ask what someone would need to read, hear or see for it to change, and picture saying it calmly, once. If you pray, offer that change to God; if you don't, simply hold the gentler plan in mind.
Erasmus. The scholar who printed the New Testament in Greek beside his own Latin, wanted scripture in every language, and hoped the Church would be reformed by learning. Today's word.
Your line: reform by learning. Patience was the whole of his wager. Day eight hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Erasmus is not a canonized saint and has no feast day; Catholics and Protestants alike read his editions, letters and satires as part of the history of reform, and scholars still argue over how to place him.

notes: Paraclesis paraphrased: farmer at the plow, weaver at the shuttle, traveler on the road; scripture translated into all languages. Confirm.

Erasmus's New Testament (Novum Instrumentum, 1516): Greek text with his Latin translation in parallel columns; 'spent years gathering old Greek manuscripts' is general. No 'first printed' claim made. Confirm phrasing.
On Free Will: subtitle 'diatribe sive collatio' (discourse or comparison) rendered as 'a discussion'; confirm. Luther's reply, The Bondage of the Will.
'Some on each side found him too cautious' and 'both sides have claimed parts of Erasmus': general historiography; confirm fair.
